topic: What if all internet stops worldwide?
title: WHAT IF THE ENTIRE
INTERNET JUST STOPPED?

power.rule: every cable, every satellite, every router — silent
power.look: a globe pulsing with light goes dark in a single frame

script.beat: 1 cold open: three vignettes of sudden silence
script.text: A surgeon in Tokyo loses the live feed guiding her scalpel. A cargo ship in the Pacific loses GPS and drifts blind. A teenager in São Paulo watches her video call freeze — then the spinner never stops. Click. Gone.
What if the entire internet just stopped? Not slowed. Not censored. Stopped. Every router, every undersea cable, every satellite link — silent at once.

script.beat: 3 the fun part: the first hour
script.text: Minute zero: memes stop mid-send. Minute three: Uber drivers pull over, maps frozen. Minute seven: stock exchanges halt — $400 billion in trades vanish into limbo. Minute fifteen: your smart fridge forgets it's a fridge. Minute thirty: the President's secure phone becomes a paperweight. Minute sixty: the world realizes — this isn't an outage. This is the new normal.

Here's what most people miss. The internet isn't the web. The web is just one app. The internet is the plumbing: BGP routes, DNS root servers, undersea cables carrying 99% of intercontinental data, time servers syncing power grids, banks, hospitals, water treatment. When the plumbing stops, civilization doesn't just lose TikTok. It loses coordination.

script.beat: 5 day one: the supply chain snaps
script.text: Just-in-time logistics runs on API calls. No internet means no port manifests, no customs clearance, no truck routing. Supermarkets have three days of food. Pharmacies have two weeks of insulin. By day three, the shelves are empty not because food vanished — because nobody knows where it is.

Ninety-two percent of money is digital entries on bank ledgers. No internet means no settlement, no ATMs, no card readers. Cash works — until it runs out. Barter returns. A can of beans becomes worth more than a Bitcoin wallet you can't open.

Wikipedia: gone. Medical journals: gone. Repair manuals for the generators keeping hospitals alive: gone. We've outsourced memory to the cloud. Without it, a generation of specialists can't pass on what they know. The doctors who remember paper charts are retiring. The engineers who knew analog switches are gone.

script.beat: 8 the science: could it actually happen?
script.text: Yes. A Carrington-class solar storm — like 1859, but today — induces DC currents that melt transformer windings globally. Or a coordinated cyberweapon targeting BGP and DNS roots simultaneously. Or a cascade failure: one root server misconfiguration propagates, DNS collapses, the web of trust unravels. Probability per decade: non-trivial. Impact: existential.
We built a civilization that assumes the wire will always hum. What happens when we're wrong?

science.claim: 99% of intercontinental data travels through undersea cables.
science.working: TeleGeography / Submarine Cable Map 2024: ~550 active cables, 1.4 million km total. Satellites carry <1% of intercontinental traffic due to latency and bandwidth limits.

science.claim: A Carrington-class solar storm would induce grid-destroying currents globally.
science.working: The 1859 Carrington Event caused telegraph lines to spark and catch fire. Modern grid transformers are vulnerable to geomagnetically induced currents (GIC). A 2013 Lloyd's/Atmospheric and Environmental Research study estimated $2.6T damage in US alone, 20-40M people without power 16-24 months.
science.source: Lloyd's 'Solar Storm Risk to the North American Electric Grid' 2013; NASEM 2021

science.claim: 92% of money is digital ledger entries.
science.working: Federal Reserve / Bank of England: M2 money supply vs physical currency in circulation. US: ~$2.3T physical vs ~$21T M2 (2024). Similar ratios globally.
science.source: Federal Reserve H.6, Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin

science.claim: Just-in-time logistics depends on continuous API connectivity.
science.working: Port operations (Terminal Operating Systems), customs (single window systems), fleet management (telematics), warehouse management — all cloud/API-based. No offline fallback in most modern deployments.
science.source: World Bank 'Digital Trade' 2022; UNCTAD 'Review of Maritime Transport' 2023
